This looks like it's using the emSign root path, which is useful, but the AAA root path is equally useful in different cases. The AAA root path was disabled for https on root stores newer than February 2025, but has been in root stores since forever. Meanwhile the emSign root path was only included in root stores since ~2018 and got removed in October 2026.So from the perspective of hacking old IoT devices, if your device hasn't been updated since 2018, the AAA path should work; if since February 2025, either path works; if since October 2026, the emSign path.reply

The state of the art for this problem is an algorithm that multiplies polynomials of degree n in time O(n log n 4^log*(n)) [HvdH19].@platypii and I obtained a Lean proof of the same improvement for DFT over prime-order finite fields (yielding polynomial multiplication via the convolution theorem): https://github.com/platypii/integer-mult-bounds-lean/blob/ma...reply

Note in this case the title says "O(n log n)", but the important part is this is "o(n log n)", not just "O(n log n)'. The former is a strict subset of the latter. We already knew how to multiply two n-bit integers in O(n log n) time, via the FFT.reply
Roughly speaking, O(n log n) means "grows no faster than k(n log n) for some k", whereas o(n log n) means grows strictly more slowly* than k(n log n) for all* choices of k.reply
For those of us uninformed, what’s the difference between O and o?reply

f(n) = O(g(n)) means as n increases, f(n)/g(n) must not grow beyond a constantf(n) = o(g(n)) means as n increases, f(n)/g(n) must shrinkreply
s/must shrink/must eventually shrink, after finitely many n/Equivalently, must go to zero in the limit.reply

title: Rust Style Guide (google.github.io)
comments: Apply #[non_exhaustive] to publicly-exposed enums seems like a crazy recommendation to me. So much of the power of enums is that when you add a new case the compiler will flag all pattern matches that you need to update, which is a good thing because you're forced to consider each case. Having a catch-all saves dev-time but it risks not appropriately handling new cases becoming a runtime issue instead of a compile time error.reply

Can anyone expand on the chromium specifc guidelines on super tiny crates, particularly no nesting of modules/source files?That feels like the ~2010 era of people saying that functions should be as small as possible.  That lead me to reviewing a lot of code where every function was one or two lines and you couldn't actually see what was going on anymore through the layers of unneeded abstraction.I want to give chrome the benefit of the doubt, but that seems really goofy.reply

In Cargo-built Rust, a crate is costly in terms of abstraction because it needs its own directory, Cargo.toml, src/ subdir, etc.  In the Google build systems I've worked with in the past (and it looks like Chromium follows) they instead put source files in the same directory mixing languages and with finer-grained libraries as they see fit.Given that a crate is the unit of build parallelization in Rust, there's a benefit to more crates especially when they don't cost much cognitive overhead.  You could imagine using crates in the way you'd typically use separate mods in a normal Rust project.I dug around in their code search to find some examples but didn't see much Rust in there, seems still early.  I think https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:tes... has ~4 Rust files that end up separate crates though.  (One of them defines a proc macro so even in a Cargo built Rust project it would need to be in its own separate crate, I think!)reply
It looks like there's some macro-based import that does import by path, so crate names are generated:https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:tes...reply

It might have to do with optimizing compile times.  A crate is the unit of compilation, so small crates increase the likelihood that you won't end up recompiling a lot of unrelated code.I guess smaller crates and avoiding nested modules could also help optimize for making the code greppable by coding agents without blowing up context windows.reply

The granularity of crates shouldn't really impact what kinds of abstractions you build. You can still have as many modules and types as you need, and as big of functions as you need, but its saying you should organize the modules into separate crates instead of one large crate. They even call out the trait coherence rules, saying that you can just make your library bigger instead of forcing a more awkward design in the pursuit of a smaller crate.I think one benefit of small crates is that it gives you more granularity in linking and dependency graphs, which is especially relevant for rebuilds. At a previous job we had a monolithic "utilities" crate, and this caused problems when you tried to depend on it for the IP address utilities but this brought in the radio frequency utilities. When one of these submodules got an update the versioning would excessively propagate downstream to every consumer. If this was organized as small "net-utils" and "rf-utils" crates then maybe it would not have been as much of an issue.reply

This being Google, I assume everything goes into a single gigantic monorepo that gets thrown at Blaze. If the unit of compilation is the crate, it makes sense for them to prefer that crates are as small as possible.reply

Maybe one or two line functions are a totally different scale than "all source code files in a crate"?  So like, one is problematic in a way the other is not.  And the guidance is "prefer small," not "always super tiny."  See: "Larger crates are allowed" later on.  And also see: "Rationale: Fine-grained library targets are recommended in Chromium due to the massive size of our codebase, non-local effects of adding dependencies in the build graph, and to improve performance of parallel compilation and build caching."reply

blaze/bazel doesn't support incremental crate compilation. It also can't, by design, as incremental compilation depends on incremental change to local build artifacts which isn't deterministic.So a single crate has to be as small as possible so builds are fast & cachable.reply

You get stricter enforcement of public APIs and dependencies. You can't import anything you haven't declared as a dep, and cycles are impossible. Rustdoc by default shows only your intended public API.OTOH if you have one crate with lots of modules, it's tempting to import anything anywhere and use pub(crate). Rustdoc needs to be configured to show private items if you want to see internal APIs.reply

title: Using LLM for confidence scoring is a bad idea (rumple.github.io)
comments: I think it's good to continually remind oneself that these are next-word/token-predictors...you can wrap them up in a harness, you can feed them into each other, you can influence the likelyhood of a given word through weights and system prompts...but that's literally all they can do.  They can't reason, but they can predict what reasoning looks like.None of this means they can't be useful tools, but when they fall down, we should remind ourselves of why that is, and be honest with ourselves about what they could ultimately be capable of.reply
What is the difference between reasoning and predicting what reasoning would look like?reply
The same as the difference between a thing and a statistical model of a thing.They don't always match up.reply
Yeah, using them for any (most) subjective task is generally incorrectreply

LLMs are bad for rating or scoring anything because they have the sensibilities of the average person... And unfortunately, the average person has poor taste.This is a tough one to explain because some people think the average person has good taste by definition. I used to think that way but over the years I've realized that a lot of what the average person likes is derivative 'slop' - This was true before AI and still true with AI.Once you start deducting points for lack of originality, you will realize that people have really poor taste... Very narrow taste. Most people literally consume trashy variations of the same thing over and over. We have to start deducting points for this because the more intelligent among us can't take it anymore! We're tired of being exposed to thousands of variants of the same slop... It might be sufficiently different to fool the average pleb's simple mind but to us it's like eating the exact same dish every day with different amounts of salt and pepper.reply
first_paragraph: Amrut Joshi, October 20, 2026LLM-based agents can do a lot of tasks. Or, at least, they can appear to do them. For example, they write code, summarize papers, plan trips, and fill in forms. If you ask one for a probability or a confidence score, it will give you one of those too. I have seen many agent designers use LLMs to generate confidence scores in this way. The problem is that there is no good reason to trust that number. This post is about why we cannot rely on an LLM to generate a confidence score.Before we can understand why an LLM cannot give a trustworthy confidence score, we need to understand what confidence really means.For example, think of a weather forecaster who says “I am 70% confident that it’s going to rain tomorrow.”The forecaster is predicting that it will rain.
